doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Explaining jazz to people who say they don't get it
summary: The salmon analogy: people feel compelled to say they know nothing about jazz, which he calls stigmatization.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: You know. But I think that part of that is — just let me think for one second — well, the thought went out of my head, it’s okay. If you wanted me to pick up the story of my life kind of thing?

Well I have a question about maybe here’s a scenario: you’re at a cocktail party and you know in conversation it comes up that you’re in jazz, and someone says, “Well jazz, I just don’t get it. When they start doing that whatever they do I guess they’re making it up. I don’t get it.” Do you have anything that you can offer that person to help them?

Yeah sure. Ninety, over ninety-five out of a hundred people that I meet, if it comes up that I’m a jazz musician or a jazz person or somehow involved with jazz and this is not hyperbole, it’s literal, way over ninety-five percent over the last forty years, “Oh I’m a jazz saxophone player.” “Really? You know I don’t know a lot about jazz – I don’t know a lot about jazz, I like some of it” or I don’t like it, but they always say I really don’t know anything. And this has really been a huge benefit to me in terms of trying to comprehend how to teach it and also how to try and build an institution like the Jazz Museum. So my first response is, “Let me ask you a question. When you go to a restaurant and order salmon, do you say to the waiter, ‘I’ll have the salmon please, you know I don’t know much about salmon. I really don’t know much about it but I’d like to order it.’” You don’t feel compelled to express your ignorance. But something about the way that jazz has evolved leads the great majority of people to express ignorance. And that’s a huge red flag and that’s something that is incumbent upon all of us to deal with, to try and de-stigmatize it. It’s been stigmatized and that’s a fact.

That there’s something to know that I don’t know. There’s nothing to know about jazz. There’s nothing to know about eating a piece of salmon. There’s nothing to know about, you know, walking down the street. There’s nothing to know about it. You like it or you don’t like it. And if you can let go of the preconceptions, if you like it and if you’re curious, maybe you’ll want to know more about it. But there’s nothing to know. I mean Jesus, there’s nothing to know about, I mean think of some of the most basic functions that we do for enjoyment in life. I mean you know when you first got into it was it because you wanted to learn something? I don’t think so. And in terms of enjoying art I really think it’s exactly the same way. Then you want to study it. Oh this happened, I didn’t like or I did like — well talk to somebody else about it. I heard this kind of jazz, boy I liked that but I didn’t like this. So it’s been hugely stigmatized.

I love that. Because I’ve had people say, “I don’t like jazz, I don’t understand it. I like Beethoven.” And I feel like saying, “Do you understand Beethoven? What do you understand about Beethoven that makes you like it?”
And I wouldn’t be that sarcastic but I like what you say.

It’s very sincere. Do you think about, when you talk about a food you like, do you say that I don’t know anything about it but I’d like to order it? And when you listen to music I mean what happened in jazz that got to the point where over nine out of ten people have to say I don’t know much about it. It’s insane.
